plan: Paired social science passages (CLD-P-ACT-R-000060), original texts on congestion pricing: Passage A (economist's case; London 2003, Stockholm 2006 trial and 2007 permanence after a vote) and Passage B (fairness of equal fees, use of revenue, limits of majority support). No congestion-pricing passage in any bank (the one SAT hit is about road widening). Ten questions, four aimed at hard (function of the vote detail, qualified position, cross-passage response, implicit agreement). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Paying for the Road (paired passages)
passages.text:
Passage A

A road is a valuable piece of land that most cities give away. At rush hour, each driver who enters a crowded street slows everyone behind, yet no driver pays for that delay. Economists have argued for decades that charging drivers for the congestion they cause would ration road space the way prices ration everything else, and two cities have put the idea to the test.

London introduced a daily charge for driving into its center in 2003. Stockholm began a trial of its own charge in 2006, and in both cities traffic in the charged zone fell sharply almost at once. Stockholm's experience is especially telling. Before the trial, most residents opposed the charge. After seven months of shorter commutes, a majority voted to keep it, and it became permanent in 2007. People who had predicted gridlock at the zone's edges found instead that many trips had simply been shifted to other hours, combined, or made by bus.

The lesson is not that a price solves every transportation problem. It is that drivers respond to prices more than they say they will, and that the benefits of a charge are easier to see once people have lived with it.

Passage B

Supporters of congestion charges like to describe them as neutral: everyone pays the same fee, and everyone benefits from faster traffic. But a fee that is the same for everyone is not the same burden for everyone. A daily charge that a lawyer barely notices can be a real cost for a home health aide who must drive between clients' houses on a schedule set by someone else.

This does not mean that charges are a mistake. It means that their fairness depends on what a city does with the money and on what alternatives it offers. A charge whose revenue improves bus service in the neighborhoods where lower-income workers live is a different policy from one whose revenue disappears into a general budget, even if the two look identical at the toll gantry.

Nor should early public support be taken as proof that a charge treats everyone well. The residents who vote in a referendum are not always the ones who bear the heaviest costs, and a policy can grow popular because it benefits the majority while asking a minority to absorb most of its burden.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.A: argue that charges work and that their benefits grow clearer with experience.
choices.B: explain why London's charge was more successful than Stockholm's.
choices.C: argue that charges can solve every transportation problem a city faces.
choices.D: describe the opposition that congestion charges face before they are adopted.

candidates.evidence: drivers respond to prices more than they say they will
candidates.explanation: Passage A explains the case for charging, reports results in London and Stockholm, and concludes that drivers respond to prices and that benefits become clearer with experience.

B.rationale: Passage A presents both as successes and calls Stockholm's experience "especially telling," without ranking them.

C.rationale: Passage A explicitly says "a price" does not solve every transportation problem.

D.rationale: Opposition is mentioned as a detail about Stockholm, not as the passage's main subject.

hints: Read the last paragraph of Passage A.
candidates.remember: A purpose answer must fit the whole passage.

candidates.stem: In Passage A, the information that a majority of Stockholm residents voted to keep the charge mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that most residents had supported the charge from the beginning.
choices.B: suggest that votes are the best way to decide transportation policy.
choices.C: support the claim that benefits become clearer with experience.
choices.D: explain why traffic in Stockholm fell sharply almost at once.

candidates.evidence: a majority voted to keep it
candidates.explanation: Residents opposed the charge before the trial and supported it after seven months of experience, which supports the passage's closing point about benefits becoming visible with experience.

A.rationale: Passage A says most residents opposed the charge before the trial.

B.rationale: Passage A does not argue for referendums as a method.

D.rationale: The fall in traffic came before the vote; the vote does not explain it.

hints: How did opinion change, and when?

strategy.explanation: Compare the residents' views before and after the trial.

candidates.remember: Connect a detail to the claim it supports.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must link a mid-passage detail to the conclusion in the last paragraph.

candidates.stem: According to Passage A, people who predicted gridlock at the edges of Stockholm's charge zone found that many trips were instead:

choices.A: rerouted through neighborhoods just outside the zone.
choices.B: canceled because drivers could not afford the charge.
choices.C: made on foot because buses were too crowded.
choices.D: moved to other hours, combined, or made by bus.

candidates.evidence: many trips had simply been shifted to other hours, combined, or made by bus
candidates.explanation: Passage A states that many trips were shifted to other hours, combined, or made by bus.

A.rationale: This is the gridlock the people predicted, not what they found.

B.rationale: Passage A does not say trips were canceled for this reason.

C.rationale: Passage A mentions buses as an alternative, not as too crowded.

hints: Find the word "gridlock" in Passage A.
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: In Passage B, the contrast between a lawyer and a home health aide mainly serves to illustrate that:

choices.A: lawyers drive into cities more often than home health aides do.
choices.B: the same charge can weigh far more heavily on some people.
choices.C: home health aides should be exempt from congestion charges.
choices.D: congestion charges reduce traffic less than their supporters claim.

candidates.evidence: a fee that is the same for everyone is not the same burden for everyone
candidates.explanation: The example follows the claim that an equal fee is not an equal burden; the aide, who must drive on someone else's schedule, feels the charge more.

A.rationale: The example concerns the burden of the charge, not how often each person drives.

C.rationale: Passage B does not propose exemptions; it discusses revenue and alternatives.

D.rationale: Passage B does not dispute that charges reduce traffic.

hints: What claim comes just before the example?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence before the example.

candidates.remember: Examples usually illustrate the claim right before them.

candidates.stem: The author of Passage B would most likely agree that a congestion charge:

choices.A: is unfair to lower-income workers no matter how it is designed.
choices.B: is fair because every driver pays exactly the same amount.
choices.C: should be adopted only after a referendum shows majority support.
choices.D: can be fair or unfair depending on its revenue use and alternatives.

candidates.evidence: their fairness depends on what a city does with the money
candidates.explanation: Passage B says charges are not a mistake but that fairness depends on how revenue is used and on available alternatives.

A.rationale: Passage B says charges are not a mistake and that fairness depends on design.

B.rationale: Passage B rejects the idea that an equal fee is an equal burden.

C.rationale: Passage B warns that majority support does not prove fairness.

hints: Does the author oppose charges or set conditions for them?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence beginning "This does not mean."

candidates.remember: A qualified position sets conditions rather than rejecting an idea.

author_checklist.hardness: The author criticizes the 'neutral' framing without opposing charges; two distractors take extreme positions.

candidates.stem: As it is used in Passage B, the word neutral most nearly means:

choices.C: refusing to take sides in a war.

candidates.explanation: Supporters call the charge "neutral" because "everyone pays the same fee," so the word means treating everyone alike.

B.rationale: This scientific sense does not fit a description of a fee.

C.rationale: This political sense does not fit a fee paid by drivers.

D.rationale: This sense applies to colors, not to a policy.

hints: What follows the word "neutral" after the colon?

strategy.explanation: Use the explanation after the colon.

candidates.remember: A colon often defines the word before it.

candidates.stem: How would the author of Passage B most likely respond to Passage A's use of the Stockholm vote?

choices.A: By agreeing that the vote proves the charge treats all residents well.
choices.B: By cautioning that majority approval does not prove costs are fairly shared.
choices.C: By arguing that the vote was invalid because many residents did not drive.
choices.D: By claiming that traffic in Stockholm did not actually decrease after the charge.

candidates.evidence: Nor should early public support be taken as proof that a charge treats everyone well.
candidates.explanation: Passage B's last paragraph directly addresses public support, warning that a policy can be popular while a minority bears most of its burden.

A.rationale: Passage B says early public support should not be taken as proof that a charge treats everyone well.

C.rationale: Passage B does not question the vote's validity or mention residents who did not drive.

D.rationale: Passage B does not dispute the traffic results.

hints: Which paragraph of Passage B discusses public support?
candidates.remember: When comparing passages, find where one addresses the other's evidence.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect Passage B's general warning to a specific detail in Passage A.

candidates.stem: Both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.A: congestion charges place an equal burden on all drivers.
choices.B: the revenue from a charge matters more than the reduction in traffic.
choices.C: congestion charges can change how people travel.
choices.D: a referendum is the best test of whether a charge is fair.

candidates.evidence: drivers respond to prices more than they say they will
candidates.explanation: Passage A reports that drivers shifted trips, and Passage B never disputes that charges change behavior; it questions who bears the cost.

A.rationale: Passage B rejects this; Passage A does not claim it.

B.rationale: Only Passage B emphasizes revenue, and neither ranks it above traffic.

D.rationale: Passage B says a referendum does not prove fairness.

hints: What does Passage B accept from Passage A without arguing?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate any claim that either author rejects.

candidates.remember: Shared ground is often what one author accepts without comment.

author_checklist.hardness: The agreement is implicit; Passage B never states it but never disputes it.

candidates.stem: According to Passage B, two charges that "look identical at the toll gantry" can differ in:

choices.A: how much traffic they remove from the city center.
choices.B: what happens to the money they raise.
choices.C: how much each driver pays to enter the zone.
choices.D: whether residents voted to approve them.

candidates.evidence: revenue disappears into a general budget
candidates.explanation: Passage B contrasts a charge whose revenue improves bus service with one whose revenue goes into a general budget.

A.rationale: Passage B does not discuss differences in traffic reduction.

C.rationale: The charges look identical, so the fee is the same.

D.rationale: Passage B discusses voting separately, not as the difference between these two charges.

hints: What does the sentence say each charge's revenue does?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: Compared with Passage A, Passage B focuses more on:

choices.A: who bears the costs of a congestion charge.
choices.C: the history of charges in London and Stockholm.
choices.D: the economic theory behind pricing road space.

candidates.evidence: a policy can grow popular because it benefits the majority while asking a minority to absorb most of its burden
candidates.explanation: Passage B centers on unequal burdens, the use of revenue, and who pays most of the cost.

B.rationale: Passage A focuses on traffic reduction; Passage B does not dispute it.

C.rationale: Passage A, not Passage B, describes these cities.

D.rationale: Passage A, not Passage B, explains the economists' argument.

hints: What is the central concern of Passage B?

strategy.explanation: State each passage's focus in a few words.

candidates.remember: Compare the focus of each passage before answering.
